storm.summary_layperson: No thunderstorm risk in the forecast window tonight — skies stay quiet, and with no marine layer or sea breeze in play, the cove behaves just like the surrounding shoreline.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Sound water (74°F) is actually warmer than the air right now, so there's no protective marine layer to speak of — moot tonight since no storms are approaching anyway.
storm.detail_html:
Instability is essentially nonexistent: CAPE sits at only 20 J/kg per the latest HRRR run, and KOKX radar shows no echoes anywhere near the cove. There are no active NWS alerts. The Area Forecast Discussion mentions a chance of strong to severe storms, but that's flagged for Sunday, not tonight's 5–10 PM window.

The Sound's usual protective mechanism — a cool marine layer that can choke off incoming storms before they reach the cove — isn't a factor tonight for a different reason: it isn't there. Water is 74.3°F versus air at 73.4°F, a negative air–water gap. The trend projection shows this gap staying negative (roughly -1°F to -3°F) through the evening; there's no meaningful buffer to build or lose.

Because there's nothing on radar and nothing in the instability numbers to suggest storm development, the local-effect question is academic tonight. The bigger story for this window is on the wind side — see below.

What would change this call: any new convective initiation showing up on KOKX radar within 50 miles, or an NWS watch/advisory being issued for the area. Neither is in play as of this run.

wind.tactics_blurb: Light ENE gradient flow (5–7 kt early, fading toward 3–4 kt after dark) with no sea breeze in play — expect patchy, unpredictable pressure as Greenwich Point casts a partial shadow. Stay central and play the puffs rather than commit to a side.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
This is a gradient-only day — light gradient wind, no sea breeze in play (internal code: B-light). The sea-breeze test needs both a land–water temperature gap of 5°F or more and a favorable gradient; neither is met. The air–water differential is actually negative (-0.9°F, water warmer than air), and the sea-breeze ensemble shows only 10% of coastal stations reading southerly — nowhere close to a building thermal. The gradient itself is light: authoritative (airport-grade) stations average just 3.3 kt, while HRRR's own forecast for the window runs a bit higher at 5–7 kt from the E/ENE.

Worth flagging: HRRR's f01 direction (76° ENE) diverges from the current western-LIS station ensemble (109° ESE) by 33°, and station-to-station direction agreement is low (0.32) — stations across the area aren't pointing the same way. That's typical of a weak, directionless gradient day rather than a real boundary or front; treat any single-station reading (including RYC's current calm/variable state) with caution.

Per the cove geography table, E and ENE flow gets partial shelter from Greenwich Point (Tod's Point) on the eastern shore, which is what's producing the patchy, uncertain pressure — but with wind this light and direction this unsettled, that shelter effect isn't reliable enough to bank on one side of the course. Expect drifter-to-light-air conditions (3–7 kt) — RC may consider a shorter course or postponement if it drops further.

HRRR's hourly model only extends through 7 PM this cycle (fetch warnings on f05 and beyond); the 8–10 PM rows above are extrapolated from the observed backing trend (E → ENE → NE) and the general B-light expectation that light gradient wind goes fully variable once the boundary layer stabilizes after dark. Confidence on direction drops noticeably for the last two hours of the window — re-check RYC live readings closer to race time rather than trusting the forecast direction blindly that late.
